Tilt the phone to light a live card

Three cards made of HTML, drawn through foil, hologram and lenticular shaders. Press "Use the phone's tilt" and tilt the phone: the cards lean and their surfaces change with the angle. Without a sensor, move the pointer or drag a finger across the panel. The buttons on the cards work while they lean. The third card has two faces and shows one or the other by angle.

How it works

  • tiltLight() writes the lean to two custom properties on the panel. The fx library passes them to each card's shader as u_xy and to the card's geometry function, which returns a perspective matrix.
  • The picture of a card is uploaded once. While the phone tilts only the two numbers change, so the foil and hologram cards cost one draw per frame and no upload.
  • The shader can't know which part of a card is the hologram. CSS paints that part magenta, and the shader replaces pixels close to magenta.
  • The lenticular card is the exception to "no upload". Its two faces are interleaved by CSS masks whose strip width is computed from --fx-x, so its picture changes with the lean and is uploaded again.
  • When the lean crosses zero the page sets data-face on the badge, which moves pointer-events to the face that shows more, and calls navigator.vibrate(8).

Findings

From Chromium 157 with software rendering and no orientation sensor. The rows above say what your browser does.

  • Works: buttons on a leaning card. The perspective matrix goes to updateElementGeometry(), and elementFromPoint() finds a button at its drawn position at full lean.
  • Works: a colour as a mask. A magenta block in the DOM is replaced by the shader. The edge of the block is one soft pixel. A card that falls back to plain HTML shows the magenta block.
  • Works: lenticular faces in CSS. mask-image with a strip width from calc() of a registered property is applied in the picture, and the picture follows the property.
  • Limit: one input face at a time. Both faces of the badge are in the same place. Which one takes a press is decided by script at the zero crossing, not by what each strip shows.
  • Not verified here: everything about the sensor. The test browser has none, so the check above sends a synthetic deviceorientation event. Open on the phone: the event rate, the latency, whether Chrome on Android asks for permission, and whether navigator.vibrate() gives a tick at the flip. The web haptics API isn't in the test browser and isn't used.
